headline: Developer builds own AI training framework Tensorless after PyTorch complexity
summary: A developer created Tensorless, a lightweight AI training framework, after finding existing tools like PyTorch too complex and bulky for simple model training. It aims to automate setup and reduce package size.
details: A developer, initially learning PyTorch, found the setup for training AI models repetitive and cumbersome. This experience sparked the idea for a more streamlined approach to machine learning workflows.

The core concept behind Tensorless was to automate most of the 'boring stuff' in model training. It aimed to allow users to simply provide training data and let the framework handle complex configurations.

Initially, Tensorless used PyTorch underneath, but the developer soon realized the dependencies could swell to over 500MB. This led to a decision to build a custom neural/training system from scratch to ensure a lightweight package.

The new custom system involved developing components for neural networks, CUDA optimization, data pipelines, and automatic configuration. The goal was to create a focused, efficient training infrastructure without unnecessary bloat.

Early experiments with a CPU-trained model showed promising, 'fun' results in language generation. However, this also highlighted the critical difference between merely running a neural network and making it learn effectively.

Tensorless offers a simple function for beginners while retaining deep configuration options for advanced users. This dual approach ensures accessibility without sacrificing control for experienced programmers.

A key design principle is maintaining a small package size, currently under 30-40 MB. This allows developers to experiment without needing to install a massive stack of components, addressing the initial frustration with larger frameworks.

headline: SkyLens launches live 3D satellite tracker with declassified Pentagon UFO archive
summary: The new platform aggregates 375 declassified UAP records from the Pentagon's PURSUE program, alongside real-time 3D tracking of every publicly cataloged Earth-orbit object.
details: SkyLens, an independent space-data and UAP-research platform, has launched with a live 3D satellite tracker and a comprehensive archive of declassified Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) records. The platform currently hosts 375 declassified records from the U.S. Department of War's PURSUE program across five releases.

The UAP archive spans from 1947 to 2026, featuring highlights like a six-clip Gulf of Oman 2021 Navy series, a five-clip Pacific Ocean 2019 series, and FBI witness interviews. It also includes digital renderings of triangular craft over Afghanistan (2002) and Colorado Springs (2023), and historical reports like the 1965 CIA object near Puerto Rico.

The real-time 3D globe renders every publicly tracked Earth-orbit object from the CelesTrak catalog, allowing users to filter by country, orbit type, launch operator, or mission category. This includes tracking for ISS, Starlink, GPS, Galileo, geostationary satellites, and low-orbit debris.

Beyond satellites and UAPs, SkyLens also offers near-Earth asteroid tracking using NASA's CNEOS and JPL SBDB feeds. Users can view 3D orbital paths in real time, complete with close-approach dates, miss distances, relative velocities, and potentially-hazardous flags.

The platform provides daily editorial coverage of space and UAP news from official public sources, alongside hand-written case files covering the full international UAP historical record. Examples include the Father Gill Papua New Guinea 1959 incident and France's GEIPAN cases.

SkyLens emphasizes its editorial independence and non-affiliation with any government agency. All data is sourced from public catalogs like CelesTrak, NASA/JPL, and official government records from war.gov, DVIDS, AARO, and FBI, with direct links provided.
